Follow the Rupee

Where Mumbai's 2025 monsoon road-repair money went, whether the fixes lasted, and where the next rupee should go.

Synthetic data. This is a hackathon prototype built on the Claude Impact Lab Mumbai dataset. It is not BMC data, and every contractor is fictional. Do not use it to judge any real person, contractor or department.

₹13.43 crspent on 2,499 repair jobs (budget ₹14.91 cr)
₹3.07 crspent on 611 fixes that failed within 30 days
623jobs flagged for review (₹3.77 cr billed)
896citizen complaints still open with no repair linked

What happened to my complaint?

For citizens. Enter a complaint number to follow it to the repair, the contractor, the cost and whether the fix lasted. Try BMC25-000295 or BMC25-000812.

Your ward

Pick a ward to see its money trail, the jobs to check, and where to spend next.

Contractor scorecards

Fair comparison: each contractor is measured against what an average contractor would get on the same mix of repair methods, low-lying wards and heavy-rain weeks. Grades use durability, speed and billing accuracy. DLP payments are not counted against contractors: they are a BMC payment check.

How we checked

Over-billed Cost is more than 1.35× the rate card for that method and area. Normal jobs vary 20 to 30% around the rate; in this data no job sits between 1.30× and 1.35×, so the line is clean.

Possible double billing A job with no complaint linked, on the same road, same method and same contractor as a real job completed within 5 days.

Paid during DLP BMC paid for a repair on a road still under its Defect Liability Period, when the original contractor should fix it for free.

Confidence. High: billed 1.5× or more, a repeat bill, or a surface repair paid during DLP. Medium: billed 1.35 to 1.5×, or drainage work on a DLP road (worth checking whether the road contract covers it). We do not flag missed deadlines or failed fixes as wrongdoing: rain and low-lying wards explain much of that, so they go into the fair scorecards instead.

Next rupee. Roads with open, unfixed complaints are ranked by risk: complaints and upvotes, nearby flood spots, traffic and bus routes, road-condition accidents, hospital and school access, and past failed fixes. The suggested method is the most durable one in the data for that issue (for potholes, hot mix fails 23% of the time vs 32% for cold mix). Roads under DLP go back to the original contractor at no cost.

Connecting the trail. 6,501 complaints in English, Hinglish, Marathi and Hindi. Each is placed on a road (by GPS for 3,777, by locality name or Devanagari alias for 2,722), its issue is re-read from the text (1,518 were filed under the wrong or a vague category), 1,014 duplicates are set aside, and the rest are followed to the 4,948 complaints BMC linked to a work order, or marked as never fixed. Open complaints on the same road and issue count as one problem.

Prototype note: the issue re-reading uses English, Hindi and Marathi keywords here; with an API key, Claude does this step and writes the scorecard text (prompt in prompts/).

Data: Claude Impact Lab Mumbai dataset (CC BY 4.0), synthetic. Checks run in Python; scorecard text written by Claude. Prototype, 21 November 2026.
